Every footnote marker shape at once

A synthetic probe carrying one of each footnote reference markup a publisher emits, so the prune rule can be re-checked against every shape it claims rather than against the single shape the real corpus article happens to use.

The GitHub and pandoc shape wraps its anchor in a superscript and marks it explicitly1 so the reference is identifiable from the attribute alone, and the sentence carries on afterwards with enough ordinary words to stay well clear of any length floor.

The Wikipedia shape puts brackets inside the anchor and classes the superscript[2] rather than the anchor, which is why the rule matches on both the wrapper and the anchor instead of on one of them.

The Substack shape has no superscript element at all and leans on a class3 to carry the meaning, so an anchor-level match is the only thing that reaches it.

A plain superscript wrapping an unclassed anchor4 is the shape a static site generator emits by default, and it is caught by the wrapper alone.

The near misses that must survive

Adopting a tool goes through phase 1 and 2 before anything useful happens, and by step 5 the habit is formed, which is a sentence full of ordinary prose numbers that mean exactly what they say and must reach the listener intact.

The author wrote it that way [sic], and the argument goes back to [Knuth 1984] and to a much older survey published in [1997], none of which is a footnote reference and all of which a reader expects to see on the page.

Reading the value at items[0] and then at items[12] is how the loop advances, and an array index written into prose like that is not a reference marker even though it is a number in brackets.

total = 0
for row in values[3]:
    total += row[0]
print(total)

The area scales as x2 and the rate is quoted in m s-1, so a superscript with no anchor inside it is load bearing prose and is deliberately left where it is.
